scenes.text: Dolphins sleep with only half of their brain at a time.
While one side rests, the other side stays awake.
The eye on the opposite side of the sleeping half usually closes.
Scientists call this unihemispheric slow wave sleep.
Each half of a bottlenose dolphin's brain gets about four hours of deep sleep a day.
The awake half helps the dolphin come up to breathe and keep watch.
Sleeping dolphins may float still at the surface or swim slowly.
Captive dolphins have even been seen sleeping on the bottom of a pool, rising for air.
In one study, each one sided sleep session lasted about forty minutes on average.
Scientists have recorded this half brain sleep in a calf only a few weeks old.
Fur seals do something similar when they sleep in the water.
Even some birds can do it. In a twenty sixteen study, great frigatebirds were recorded sleeping in mid air on long flights over the ocean.
Mallard ducks at the edge of a group sleep with their open eye facing outward, watching for predators.
It lets these animals rest without ever fully switching off.
If half your brain could stay awake, what would you use it for? Comment below.

title: Dolphins sleep with half their brain 🐬
caption: Dolphins rest one brain half at a time, usually with the opposite eye closed, so they can keep surfacing to breathe. Fur seals, ducks and even flying frigatebirds do a version of it too.
